title: Bitcoin
headline: Meet Bitcoin. Then drive it.
summary: Start with how Bitcoin works in plain pictures, then receive, prove, send, and guard the keys. Play money. About 35 minutes.
coachPitch: By the end you know what Bitcoin is, you can receive it, prove it arrived, and send a small amount without giving your keys away.

drives.title: What Bitcoin is
drives.job: Meet the protocol before you touch a wallet
drives.outcome: What Bitcoin is and why it matters — you'll explain scarcity, blocks, and sats in plain words.

steps.coachLine: Satoshi published the idea in 2008. The network started in 2009. No company runs it.
steps.button: Show me how scarce it is
steps.ideaBody: In 2008 someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a short paper describing Bitcoin. In 2009 the network went live. No company sits in the driver's seat.
steps.objective: After this screen you can say who started Bitcoin and that it is an open network, not a bank product.
steps.whyItMatters: Pros meet "Bitcoin" in policy decks. Knowing it began as a public paper and a live network stops the myth that a single vendor runs it.
steps.misconception: Bitcoin is a company you can call for support.

steps.coachLine: Only 21 million bitcoin will ever exist. That is the scarce part.
steps.ideaBody: Only 21 million bitcoin will ever exist. New coins arrive on a schedule. The supply does not stretch when demand rises.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain the 21 million hard cap in one plain sentence.
steps.whyItMatters: Scarcity is why people treat bitcoin differently from a bank balance that can be inflated by policy.
steps.misconception: Miners can print as much bitcoin as they want whenever they like.

steps.coachLine: About every ten minutes, a page of payments is sealed. The miner who seals it is paid new bitcoin.
steps.button: Does that pay stay the same?
steps.ideaBody: About every ten minutes, a new block of payments is sealed. The miner who seals it earns new bitcoin as the pay for that work.
steps.objective: After this screen you can describe a block as a sealed page of payments that arrives on a roughly ten-minute rhythm.
steps.whyItMatters: Waiting for a payment is waiting for that page to seal — not waiting for a bank clerk.
steps.misconception: Bitcoin payments clear instantly like a card swipe every time.

steps.job: The pay gets cut in half
steps.coachLine: That pay is cut in half on a schedule. New coins slow down. Scarcity holds.
steps.ideaBody: The miner's new-coin pay is cut in half on a fixed schedule. New supply slows. The hard cap still holds.
steps.objective: After this screen you can say that miner rewards shrink over time on a schedule (halving).
steps.whyItMatters: Issuance is mechanical, not a board decision. That is part of the scarcity story.
steps.misconception: Someone can vote to mint unlimited new bitcoin next quarter.

steps.coachLine: One bitcoin is 100,000,000 satoshis. People usually send sats, not whole coins.
steps.ideaBody: One bitcoin is 100,000,000 satoshis. Everyday sends are usually counted in sats, not whole coins.
steps.objective: After this screen you can convert the idea "1 BTC = 100,000,000 sats" and know why small amounts still make sense.
steps.whyItMatters: Pros see tiny decimals on invoices. Sats are the cents — that is normal, not a glitch.
steps.misconception: You can only send whole bitcoin.

steps.coachLine: Your balance is not an account. It is unspent cheques. Add them up.
steps.pocketCard: Balance = the total of your unspent cheques (UTXOs).
steps.ideaBody: Your balance is not a bank account line. It is the total of unspent cheques (UTXOs) you can still sign. Add them up to see what you hold.
steps.objective: After this screen you can treat balance as the sum of unspent cheques, not a single account field.
steps.whyItMatters: Explains change, coin selection, and why "the wallet shows 0.01" can mean several pieces.
steps.misconception: Bitcoin works like a single running account balance at a bank.

steps.coachLine: You sign one cheque. They get a new cheque. The leftover comes back to you as a new cheque.
steps.button: Got it — let me get paid
steps.pocketCard: Spend signs a cheque. Change comes back to you. Play money from here.
steps.ideaBody: You sign one cheque. They receive a new cheque. The leftover returns to you as a new cheque. The toll peels off as a fee.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain pay + change + fee when spending from an unspent cheque.
steps.whyItMatters: Stops panic when a send "uses" a larger piece than the invoice — change comes back.
steps.misconception: If you spend from a 1 BTC cheque to pay 0.1, the other 0.9 disappears.

drives.title: Get paid
drives.job: Receive a payment and prove it arrived
drives.outcome: Getting paid in bitcoin — you'll share an address safely and prove a payment landed.

steps.job: Give them a place to send
steps.coachLine: The address is the license plate. The key stays in your pocket.
steps.ideaBody: Your Bitcoin address is safe to hand out; it can receive payments but cannot spend them. Spending needs the key, which never leaves your pocket. Many wallets hand you a fresh address for each payment so your receipts stay unlinkable.
steps.objective: After this screen you can share a Bitcoin address to receive a payment while keeping the key private.
steps.whyItMatters: Client onboarding often stalls on the fear that sharing an address leaks control; it does not — control stays with the key.
steps.misconception: Sharing your address gives the other person a way to take your bitcoin.

steps.coachLine: A screenshot is not proof. This page is the receipt.
steps.pocketCard: Address = plate. Explorer = receipt. 3 confirms = landed.
steps.ideaBody: A payment lands when the network seals it into blocks, one confirmation per block. Wallets usually treat a few confirmations as settled; this course uses three. Until then, the money is announced, not arrived.
steps.objective: After this screen you can read a receipt page and say whether a payment has reached three confirmations.
steps.whyItMatters: Settlement finality is what a treasurer is really asking about; confirmations are how Bitcoin answers.
steps.misconception: A payment is final the moment your wallet shows it as incoming.

steps.job: Prove it arrived — the real receipt
steps.coachLine: Every Bitcoin transaction has a public receipt. Let's read one — a real one, already confirmed. Your earlier practice receipt stayed simulated.
steps.ideaBody: A txid is a 64-character fingerprint of a transaction. This link opens the well-known 2010 Bitcoin pizza payment on mainnet. You read a public ledger page — not a screenshot from a chat.
steps.objective: After this screen you can open a txid on mempool.space and find status, confirmations, block height, fee rate (sat/vB), inputs, outputs, and addresses.
steps.whyItMatters: When someone pays you, the explorer — not a JPG — is how you prove it landed.
steps.misconception: A payment screenshot in chat is as good as an explorer receipt.
steps.pocketCard: txid → explorer → status, confirms, block, fee rate, inputs, outputs. Looking up your own addresses on a public site leaks privacy — prefer your own node for real use. Personal drills in this course stay play money.

drives.title: Send a little
drives.job: Send a tiny test before any real amount
drives.outcome: Sending without fear — you'll catch swapped addresses and leave room for the toll.

steps.coachLine: The start can match. Read the end before you trust a paste.
steps.pocketCard: Read the start and the end. Never trust the paste alone.
steps.ideaBody: Malware on a computer can quietly replace a pasted address with the attacker's own. The first characters often match on purpose, so a glance is not enough. You compare the start and the end against the address your recipient gave you, character by character.
steps.objective: After this screen you can spot a swapped paste by comparing the first and last characters with the intended address.
steps.whyItMatters: Payment-detail fraud is a familiar compliance headache; on Bitcoin there is no bank to reverse it, so the check happens before you press send.
steps.misconception: If the first few characters match, the pasted address must be the right one.

steps.coachLine: The fee is a toll for the road, not a bank charge.
steps.pocketCard: Leave room for the toll, or the send cannot leave.
steps.ideaBody: Every send carries a small fee that pays miners to include it in a block. The fee comes out of the same unspent cheque as the payment, so the total must cover both. If nothing is left for the toll, the send cannot leave your wallet.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain why a send needs the payment amount plus a fee to leave the wallet.
steps.whyItMatters: Clients often ask why the debited total exceeds the invoice; the fee is the toll, and it is set by the market for block space, not by a bank.
steps.misconception: The fee is a percentage the wallet company takes from your send.

steps.coachLine: On an exchange this button says Withdraw and they can delay it. In your own wallet, you press send.
steps.pocketCard: You pressed send. It does not come back.
steps.ideaBody: Once the network confirms your send, no support desk can reverse it. That is the trade for holding your own keys: nobody can freeze your money, and nobody can fetch it back. So the habit is small test first, real amount second.
steps.objective: After this screen you can list the three things to check before pressing send: address, amount, and fee.
steps.whyItMatters: Final settlement without a dispute process changes the risk model; controls move from chargebacks to pre-send checks.
steps.misconception: If you send to the wrong address, Bitcoin support can reverse it like a bank transfer.

drives.title: Guard the car
drives.job: See what the key does, then back up the words
drives.outcome: Guarding your coins — you'll separate plate from key and seal 12 words on paper.

steps.coachLine: Your exchange password is not this key. The exchange holds the real one.
steps.ideaBody: The address is the plate: public, shareable, receive-only. The key is what signs spends, and whoever holds it holds the bitcoin. On an exchange, the exchange holds the key; in your own wallet, you do.
steps.objective: After this screen you can say who controls bitcoin in each case: exchange account versus your own wallet.
steps.whyItMatters: Custody is the first question in any institutional discussion; this is the difference between an IOU and actual control.
steps.misconception: Your exchange login password is your Bitcoin private key.

steps.coachLine: Anyone with the words owns the wallet.
steps.pocketCard: Paper. Two places. Never a photo.
steps.ideaBody: The 12-word list is a backup of every key in your wallet. Anyone who reads the words can rebuild the wallet and spend from it. So the words live on paper in two places, never in a photo or a chat.
steps.objective: After this screen you can store a 12-word backup on paper in two places without photographing or typing it.
steps.whyItMatters: Key backup is the operational risk clients underestimate most; paper in two places beats every clever digital shortcut.
steps.misconception: A photo of the word list in cloud storage is a safe backup.

drives.title: Road test
drives.outcome: The road test — you'll refuse scams, pick the right network, and stop a bad send.

steps.coachLine: Nobody real needs those words.
steps.ideaBody: Scammers pose as support staff and ask for your word list to 'verify' your wallet. No real helper needs those words for any reason, ever. The correct move is to close the chat and say nothing.
steps.objective: After this screen you can refuse a support chat that asks for your word list by closing it without sharing anything.
steps.whyItMatters: Social engineering, not cryptography, is how most client funds are lost; staff who know this script protect the firm.
steps.misconception: A support agent may legitimately need your words to fix a stuck wallet.

steps.coachLine: If it starts with 0x, that is not Bitcoin.
steps.ideaBody: Each network has its own address format, and coins sent to the wrong format can be lost. Addresses starting with 0x belong to a different road, not Bitcoin. Before every send, you confirm the network matches the coin.
steps.objective: After this screen you can reject a 0x address on a Bitcoin send and switch to the Bitcoin network.
steps.whyItMatters: Wrong-network sends are unrecoverable, so network checks belong in every payment procedure alongside amount checks.
steps.misconception: All addresses work on all networks, so a 0x address is fine for Bitcoin.

steps.coachLine: Verify twice. Send once.
steps.ideaBody: When the address on screen differs from the one your recipient gave you, the send stops — no exceptions. A single changed character sends your bitcoin somewhere it cannot come back from. You re-check the source, fix the address, and only then continue.
steps.objective: After this screen you can halt a send on an address mismatch and re-verify against the recipient's original address.
steps.whyItMatters: A maker-checker habit on addresses is the cheapest control a finance team can adopt for Bitcoin payments.
steps.misconception: One wrong character is harmless because the network will correct the address.

drives.title: Prove you can drive
drives.outcome: The professional capstone — you'll verify a real payment, set a confirmation policy, choose a custody model, and defend Bitcoin to a non-technical executive.

steps.title: Prove it arrived — on a real chain
steps.coachLine: Every confirmed payment has a public receipt. We looked at one already. Now read one yourself — this is the exact skill an auditor uses.
steps.ideaBody: Verification means not trusting the sender's screenshot. You take the transaction ID, open a public explorer, and read the facts: is it confirmed, how many confirmations, what fee was paid, which addresses moved value. Anyone can do this. No account, no permission, no middleman.
steps.objective: After this screen you can independently verify any Bitcoin payment using only a txid and a public explorer.
steps.whyItMatters: Every reconciliation, audit, and dispute you'll ever handle starts here. If you can't verify a payment, you can't book it.
steps.misconception: Senders don't need to prove they paid. The chain proves it — you just have to know where to look.
steps.pocketCard: Verify the txid, not the sender's word.

quickCheck.question: What is the minimum you need to independently verify a Bitcoin payment?
options: The sender's phone number and a screenshot
The transaction ID and a public explorer
The sender's private key
A bank statement showing the transfer
quickCheck.explanation: A txid plus any public explorer is enough — no account or permission needed.

steps.title: When is a payment final?
steps.coachLine: Bitcoin doesn't have a final stamp. It has a probability curve. You decide how many blocks is enough — based on what the payment is for.
steps.ideaBody: A confirmed block is expensive to reverse. Each additional block makes reversal exponentially harder. So the question isn't 'is it final?' — it's 'how many confirmations do I need for this amount, this counterparty, this risk?' A coffee vendor takes zero. A house deposit waits six.
steps.objective: After this screen you can set a confirmation threshold that matches the value and reversibility of what you're selling.
steps.whyItMatters: Your confirmation policy is the single most important risk decision you'll make about Bitcoin in an operational setting.
steps.misconception: Confirmations are not 'approval'. Nobody approves — blocks just make reversal more expensive every ten minutes.
steps.pocketCard: Match confirmations to the cost of being wrong.

quickCheck.question: A $20 coffee vs a $200,000 house deposit — which needs more confirmations?
options: The coffee — small payments reverse more easily
The house deposit — higher amount, higher reversal cost
Neither — one confirmation is always enough
Both need exactly six
quickCheck.explanation: Match confirmations to the cost of being wrong: coffee takes zero, a house deposit waits six.

steps.title: Who holds the keys?
steps.coachLine: Self-custody isn't the only answer. For a company, it's rarely the right one alone. Compare the four models a professional actually chooses between.
steps.ideaTitle: Custody is a trade, not a rule
steps.ideaBody: Exchange, self-custody, institutional custodian, multi-sig. Each makes a different trade between convenience, control, recoverability, and legal exposure. None is 'correct' — the right choice depends on who in your organisation needs to sign, what your regulator asks for, and what happens if a key holder dies.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain the custody tradeoffs of four models to a board or regulator.
steps.whyItMatters: Custody is the decision your CFO will ask you about first. If you can't answer in one minute, you're not ready to hold Bitcoin on a balance sheet.
steps.misconception: Multi-sig is not 'more secure'. It's a different tradeoff — harder to lose, harder to move, more people who can leak.
steps.pocketCard: The right custody model is the one your board can defend.

quickCheck.question: Which model eliminates the risk of a single key holder losing access?
options: Exchange custody
Self-custody
Multi-sig — no single key can spend or be lost alone
A paper backup in one safe
quickCheck.explanation: Multi-sig spreads signing across holders, so no one person can lose the funds alone.

steps.title: What did it cost?
steps.coachLine: Every transaction competes for space in the next block. The fee you bid decides whether you wait or pay. Match the fee to the urgency — not to your mood.
steps.ideaBody: Blocks are full. Miners pick the highest bidders. When the mempool is quiet, 1 sat/vB is enough. When it's crowded, you'll pay 50 or 100. For a payroll batch you can wait — batching one transaction per batch saves fees across the whole run. For a single urgent payment, you pay the market rate.
steps.objective: After this screen you can choose a fee strategy that matches the urgency, the amount, and the budget.
steps.whyItMatters: Fees are a line item. A professional treats them like any other cost — predictable, budgeted, justifiable.
steps.misconception: Fees are not 'the network taking a cut'. Miners collect them; the amount is a market price for block space.
steps.pocketCard: Match the fee to the clock, not the panic.

quickCheck.question: Payroll runs tomorrow. One urgent supplier payment must land in an hour. Which gets the higher fee?
options: The payroll batch — more recipients cost more
The supplier payment — higher urgency justifies higher fee
Both pay the same standard fee
Neither — fees are optional
quickCheck.explanation: Match the fee to the clock: the urgent single send pays priority, the batch waits for economy.

steps.title: Get your wallet back
steps.coachLine: A backup you've never restored isn't a backup — it's a hope. Enter your twelve words now, into a fresh wallet, and watch the balance come back.
steps.ideaBody: Your twelve words are the wallet. Any compatible wallet, on any device, will regenerate the same keys — and see the same balance — from those twelve words alone. If your hardware dies, the words are what remain. If someone else gets them, they get the wallet.
steps.objective: After this screen you can restore a Bitcoin wallet from its twelve-word backup and know the process works.
steps.whyItMatters: You cannot honestly tell a board that your Bitcoin is safe unless you've restored it once yourself.
steps.misconception: The hardware wallet is not the wallet. It's a signing device. The seed phrase is the wallet.
steps.pocketCard: Restore it once or it isn't a backup.

quickCheck.question: Where do you restore a wallet from?
options: Any compatible wallet, using the twelve seed words
The original hardware device only
Your exchange account dashboard
A backup email from the wallet company
quickCheck.explanation: The seed words regenerate the same keys in any compatible wallet.

steps.title: Explain it to your CFO
steps.coachLine: Your CFO asks: 'Why should we accept Bitcoin?' You have three sentences. No hype, no price, no investment talk. Why does this matter to the business?

cert.certMilestoneLabel: Can receive, verify, send, and custody Bitcoin. Can explain Bitcoin's role to a non-technical stakeholder.

steps.ideaBody: If you can't explain Bitcoin to a non-technical executive in three sentences, you haven't learned it — you've memorised it. A defensible answer names what it is (settlement, not speculation), why it's scarce (fixed supply, published code), and how it's custodied (a decision you've made, not a default). Price and 'investment' have no place in an operational conversation.
steps.objective: After this screen you can defend Bitcoin adoption to a non-technical executive in three sentences.
steps.whyItMatters: This is the sentence your CFO repeats to the board. Write it carefully.
steps.misconception: Bitcoin is not a technology pitch. It's a policy decision — like accepting any other foreign currency.

quickCheck.question: Which of these belongs in a three-sentence CFO answer?
options: Price targets and expected returns
Scarcity, settlement, custody — not price or investment
Mining hardware recommendations
Trading strategies for volatility
quickCheck.explanation: An operational answer covers scarcity, settlement, and custody — never price or investment.
